issues.legal_issue: A court may not grant relief in a writ proceeding on a new factual and legal basis that was not pleaded.
material_facts: The writ petitions challenged the dismissal of applications opposing auction of two plots, on the ground that the applicants’ transferor had no valid title.
The applicants did not plead reliance on the later government letter concerning regularization and did not seek amendment of their pleadings.
The High Court nevertheless granted relief on the basis of that letter.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred by granting relief on an altogether new, unpleaded case; its judgment was set aside and the writ petitions were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Relief must be founded on the case pleaded by the parties. The Court relied on no specific statutory provision or earlier case for this procedural conclusion.

predicates.writ_proceeding: A party brought a writ proceeding seeking relief from an administrative or tribunal decision.
predicates.relief_basis_not_pleaded: The ground on which relief was granted was not set out in the party’s pleadings.
predicates.no_pleading_amendment_sought: The party did not ask to amend its pleadings to include that ground.

issues.definition: When relief in a writ proceeding rests on a ground absent from the pleadings and no amendment was sought, relief must not be granted on that ground.

issues.legal_issue: A departmental communication that is neither expressed in the Governor’s name nor authenticated as required cannot be treated as a government policy decision.
material_facts: A ministerial committee recommended measures to regularize constructions and occupations involving acquired land.
A departmental official sent a letter describing the committee’s recommendations and decisions.
The letter was not expressed in the Governor’s name and was not authenticated in the prescribed manner.
No material showed that the committee’s recommendations had been approved by the State Government.
issues.conclusion: The letter could not be treated as a policy decision of the State Government.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 166(1) and 166(2) of the Constitution require executive action to be expressed in the Governor’s name and orders and instruments to be authenticated as prescribed; Article 166(3) concerns rules for the transaction of government business. Relying on State of Bihar v. Kripalu Shankar (1987) 3 SCC 34, the Court held that a departmental communication lacking these features is not a government order.

rule.if: government_policy_review and departmental_communication_only and not expressed_in_governor_name and not authenticated_as_prescribed

predicates.government_policy_review: A court is asked to determine whether a communication represents a government policy decision.
predicates.departmental_communication_only: The asserted decision appears only in a communication from a departmental official describing recommendations or discussions.
predicates.expressed_in_governor_name: The communication expresses the executive action in the Governor’s name.
predicates.authenticated_as_prescribed: The communication is authenticated in the manner prescribed for government orders.

issues.definition: In a review of an asserted government policy, a departmental communication alone is not binding government policy when it is neither expressed in the Governor’s name nor authenticated as prescribed.

issues.legal_issue: A government policy cannot validate allotments or transfers of acquired land that binding Supreme Court rulings have held unlawful.
material_facts: The proposed regularization measures concerned land acquired for a public development scheme and allotments made to awardees, transferees, and their nominees.

Earlier Supreme Court rulings had held that the acquisition officer lacked authority to allot acquired land in lieu of compensation and that post-notification transfers did not confer the claimed rights.
The regularization measures would have given effect to transactions and allotments held unlawful by those rulings.
issues.conclusion: The purported policy was contrary to the law declared by the Supreme Court and could not be used to regularize the unlawful transactions; the State and the development authority were restrained from acting on the letter.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 31(3) and 31(4) of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953 did not authorize allotment of acquired land in lieu of compensation except in the limited circumstances described for a person with a limited interest. The Court relied on Jaipur Development Authority v. Radhey Shyam (1994) 4 SCC 370 and Secretary, Jaipur Development Authority v. Daulat Mal Jain (1997) 1 SCC 35, which held the relevant allotments and post-notification transactions unlawful, and on Narpat Singh v. Jaipur Development Authority (2002) 4 SCC 666.

predicates.regularization_policy_review: A court is asked to review a policy intended to regularize land allotments or occupations.
predicates.policy_covers_acquired_land_transactions: The policy would regularize transactions or allotments involving land acquired for a public purpose.
predicates.binding_rulings_hold_those_transactions_: Earlier binding court rulings have held the relevant kind of allotment or transfer unlawful.

issues.definition: A regularization policy cannot validate acquired-land transactions when binding rulings have held those transactions unlawful.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser cannot obtain enforceable title through a transferor whose claimed interest derives from a post-notification purchase and an unauthorized allotment of acquired land.
material_facts: The transferor purchased land after publication of the acquisition notification.
The transferor’s claimed interest in the plots depended on an acquisition award and a later allotment of acquired land to him.
The applicants purchased the plots from that transferor.
The Tribunal and trial court found that the transferor had no valid title, and those findings were not successfully challenged.
issues.conclusion: The transferor could not convey valid title to the applicants, who therefore had no right to prevent the development authority from auctioning the plots; the High Court erred in granting them relief.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 4 and 6 and Section 31 of the Rajasthan Land Acquisition Act, 1953, the acquisition officer had no authority to allot acquired land in the circumstances described. Such an allotment was a nullity, and a post-notification purchase did not create title. The Court relied on Jaipur Development Authority v. Radhey Shyam (1994) 4 SCC 370 and Secretary, Jaipur Development Authority v. Daulat Mal Jain (1997) 1 SCC 35, as well as Narpat Singh v. Jaipur Development Authority (2002) 4 SCC 666 on the invalidity of such directions and their enforcement.

rule.if: auction_challenge_proceeding and acquisition_notice_preceded_transfer and transferor_claim_depended_on_unauthorized_acquired_land_allotment and purchaser_claims_through_transferor

predicates.auction_challenge_proceeding: A party challenges an authority’s proposed auction of land.
predicates.acquisition_notice_preceded_transfer: The transferor’s purchase occurred after public notice that the land was to be acquired.
predicates.transferor_claim_depended_on_unauthorize: The transferor’s claimed interest depended on an award or allotment of acquired land made without authority.
predicates.purchaser_claims_through_transferor: The party challenging the auction claims its interest through a transfer from that transferor.

issues.definition: A purchaser challenging an auction has no enforceable title through a transferor whose interest depends on a post-notification purchase and an unauthorized allotment of acquired land.

issues.legal_issue: Article 14 does not entitle a person to retain or obtain an unlawful benefit merely because others obtained similar benefits.
material_facts: Some beneficiaries of the impugned allotment arrangements had received plots or possession.
The applicants relied on the treatment of other persons and on later regularization measures to claim comparable relief.
The asserted benefits arose from allotments or transactions already held unlawful.
issues.conclusion: The applicants could not claim regularization or equal treatment by relying on unlawful benefits conferred on others.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 protects persons who have a legal and valid right and does not require repetition or continuation of illegal or ultra vires acts. The Court relied on Secretary, Jaipur Development Authority v. Daulat Mal Jain (1997) 1 SCC 35, which rejected the use of equality to legitimize unlawful allotments.

predicates.equal_treatment_claim: A person seeks the same treatment or benefit given to other persons said to be similarly situated.
predicates.claimed_comparator_benefit_is_unlawful: The benefit relied on was conferred through an unlawful or ultra vires act.

issues.definition: When a person seeks equal treatment based on an unlawful benefit received by others, Article 14 does not require that unlawful benefit to be extended or preserved.
